title: Pursuing those responsible for the collapse of Shield and First Guardian is a key objective for ASIC, shaping its priorities for the next year.read more
full_text:
Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) chair Sarah Court has stated the pursuit of those responsible for the failure of the Shield and First Guardian master funds highlights the extent of action the regulator will take and how it will proceed in 2027.
Speaking at the ASIC Annual Forum in Sydney today, Court said: “Few matters better demonstrate the breadth of ASIC’s enforcement work than our response to the collapse of the Shield and First Guardian master funds. It remains one of our largest and most complex enforcement cases.
“To date, ASIC has launched 27 investigations and commenced 19 Federal Court proceedings against 38 defendants. More than $420 million has been returned for approximately 4000 affected investors.
“Our action spans advice firms and licensees, lead generators, superannuation trustees, auditors, responsible entities and officeholders.
“The collapses expose issues beyond the two funds, including conflicted advice, weaknesses in trustee and managed investment scheme governance, and failures by auditors and other gatekeepers.”
She added a range of investigations, including the ongoing work with Shield and First Guardian, had shaped the regulator’s priorities for the next year, which included harmful financial advice and lead generation models.
“We will examine the commercial arrangements driving recommendations, referrals and product distribution, and act where those arrangements place commercial interests ahead of clients. This work will complement the government’s reforms to the regulation of financial advice and lead generation,” she stated.
This examination would continue alongside further work into the collapse of Shield and First Guardian.
“This work is unfinished and its scale and complexity will continue to demand substantial enforcement attention. Investigations are continuing and further civil or criminal action will be considered where the evidence supports it,” Court said.
“As chair, I remain firmly committed to enforcement that is visible and consequential.
“The priorities for 2027 identify where greater scrutiny is now required and where industry should expect ASIC to act.”
The SMSF Association also flagged to its members that ASIC still has several regulatory funding announcements to make before the end of year, including the ASIC 2025/26 industry funding levy, the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort base levy for 2027/28 and consultation on changes to the AUSTRAC industry contribution levy following the commencement of tranche 2 of the anti-money laundering/counter-terrorism funding reforms earlier this year.
“Taken together, these developments highlight the growing importance of considering the cumulative cost of regulation, rather than examining individual levies and funding arrangements in isolation,” the association stated in a member communication.
“This was a key issue raised by the association in a recent meeting with the Department of Home Affairs in Canberra, where we emphasised the need for government to consider the cumulative impact of regulatory funding arrangements across the sector.
“Regulatory agencies and consumer protection mechanisms need to be appropriately funded, but the way those costs are allocated must also be fair, transparent and proportionate.”
author: Jason Spits
